title: Bipartisan Senate Deal Aims to Speed Up Energy Project Approvals
summary:
Senators from both parties announced Wednesday they have reached a bipartisan deal on legislation to speed up permitting reviews for new energy and infrastructure projects — projects that currently face yearslong delays.

The bill would cut down the timeline for getting big energy projects approved at a time when demand for electricity is rising, partly because of mushrooming data centers for AI. It would also require data centers to pay for the increased electricity they use, rather than leaving that cost to families.

Republican Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, who chairs the Environment and Public Works Committee, called the bill 'a major step toward making it faster and more efficient and easier to build infrastructure projects' while maintaining environmental protections. She was joined by Republican Sen. Mike Lee of Utah and Democratic Sens. Martin Heinrich of New Mexico and Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island.

Heinrich said the bill 'will mean more energy on the grid, more good-paying jobs, and lower electricity costs for families and businesses.'

But the deal faces criticism. Brad Campbell, president of the Conservation Law Foundation, said it 'appears to adopt a fossil fuel industry wish-list' and could roll back clean water and endangered species protections, limit judicial review, and curtail the EPA's power.

A vote won't happen until after the midterm elections in November. Lee said he is confident it will pass in a lame-duck session, noting support from business and environmental groups. Whitehouse said Democrats still want clarity on how the bill will prevent the Trump administration from blocking wind and solar projects. The administration suspended five offshore wind projects in December, citing national security concerns; the projects later moved forward after federal judges intervened.

The Senate bill would limit legal challenges under the National Environmental Policy Act and the National Historic Preservation Act.
why_it_matters: The rules for approving power plants and power lines decide how fast the country can add electricity for AI, electric cars and homes — so a bill like this shapes both the climate and what families end up paying on their utility bills.

background_read: The deal was shaped by Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (a Republican from West Virginia who leads the Senate committee that handles environmental policy) and Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (a Democrat from Rhode Island who has spent years pushing Congress to act on climate change).

The bill would change a law called the National Environmental Policy Act, or NEPA — a landmark 1970 law that requires the government to study how a big project might harm the environment before it is approved. Supporters of permitting reform argue that NEPA reviews can tie a project up in court for a decade; opponents answer that those reviews are often the only chance nearby communities and wildlife have to be heard.
Brad Campbell, quoted in the story, leads the Conservation Law Foundation, a nonprofit environmental law group based in New England.

Congress has tried and failed several times in recent years to pass big permitting changes, which is part of why a bipartisan agreement is unusual. The midterm elections in November will decide which party controls the Senate, and the 'lame-duck' stretch afterward — before new members are sworn in — is often when hard deals finally get pushed through.

perspectives.description: Capito, Lee, Heinrich and Whitehouse say the deal keeps environmental protections while making it faster and easier to build. They argue it will put more energy on the grid, create good-paying jobs and lower electricity costs for families and businesses.

Brad Campbell of the Conservation Law Foundation calls the deal a 'fossil fuel industry wish-list'. He warns it could weaken clean water and endangered species protections, limit judicial review and cut back the EPA's authority.

Permitting fights have run for decades: NEPA has required environmental reviews since 1970, and Congress has repeatedly tried and failed to rewrite it. Both parties want projects built faster but disagree sharply about which projects should benefit and how much say courts and communities keep.

Everything now depends on the lame-duck session after the November midterms. Democrats are still pressing for guarantees that the administration cannot single out wind and solar projects, so the bill's final shape — and whether it passes at all — remains open.
